# 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods

Using Monte Carlo simulation to get the distribution of wealth; mean, median and the probability of reaching a goal; how model assumptions and parameter uncertainty matter; backtests and their common biases.

Key file: https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/ai/en/lessons/4.13-key.md

## Monte Carlo simulation

Planning questions are often about the distribution of outcomes rather than one expected value: what range might wealth fall in after 30 years? What is the probability of reaching the retirement goal? With saving and withdrawals, such questions are hard to answer with formulas. **Monte Carlo simulation** generates many (say 10,000) return paths at random from an assumed return distribution, computes how wealth evolves on each path, and then tallies the distribution of final wealth.

The simplest assumption is that yearly log returns are independent and normal with mean $\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}$ (Lesson 4.1, "Measuring Return and Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-1-risk-return-measures/). Then wealth per dollar after $t$ years is lognormal, and its percentiles can be computed directly:

$$
W_t = \exp\!\left(\left(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)t + z\,\sigma\sqrt{t}\right), \qquad E[W_t] = e^{\mu t}
$$

$z$ is a quantile of the standard normal distribution. Figure 1-1 is drawn from this formula; once yearly saving or withdrawals are added, simulation is needed.

**Figure 1-1** The distribution of wealth per dollar invested over 30 years when yearly log returns are independent and normal. The solid line is the median, the dashed line the mean, and the dark and light areas the ranges between the 25% and 75% and between the 5% and 95% percentiles.
- This figure has no drawing instructions yet: give the learner the link to the web page and say what to change and what to observe.
- What the learner should observe: Keep the mean return fixed, raise the volatility from 18% to 30%, and compare how the median and the mean change.
- Interactive figure on the web page (the learner can also open it): https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-13-simulation-backtesting/#fig-1-1

Lesson 0.4, "Distributions and Statistical Inference" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-4-distributions-inference/#mean-median showed that the mean of a lognormal distribution is above its median. Using the mean to describe the "typical" outcome in planning makes people too optimistic (Exercises Question 1).

## How the assumptions matter

A simulation's results depend entirely on the assumptions put in:

- The distribution: the normal distribution understates how often extreme falls happen (Lesson 0.4, "Distributions and Statistical Inference" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-4-distributions-inference/#fat-tails). An alternative is the **bootstrap**: draw returns at random, with replacement, from historical years, keeping the fat tails of historical data; drawing blocks of consecutive years (the block bootstrap) also keeps the correlation between returns.
- The parameters: the expected return itself has a large estimation error (Lesson 4.10, "Estimation Error and Robust Optimization" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-10-estimation-error/). If the simulation treats $\mu$ as known, the distribution of outcomes is too narrow. Adding parameter uncertainty to the simulation (each path first draws a $\mu$) makes the range of long-run outcomes noticeably wider (Exercises Question 2).
- Correlations and inflation: the correlation between stocks and bonds changes (Lesson 2.8, "Business Cycles and Asset Prices" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-8-business-cycle-asset-prices/), and nominal and real returns must be kept apart.

> **Check question C3**
> 
> Compared with resampling historical years (the bootstrap), simulating annual returns from a normal distribution, even with the same mean and volatility, is most likely to understate:
> 
> (A) How often extreme falls happen
> (B) The average return
> (C) The volatility
> (D) The share of years with positive returns
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

What a simulation can do is work out the implications of the assumptions, not remove uncertainty. When the inputs are unreliable, a success probability given to decimal places is false precision; it is more useful to compare whether the conclusion changes under different assumptions.

## Backtesting

A **backtest** tests an investment strategy on historical data: suppose one had traded by the strategy's rules in the past, and compute the result. Backtests easily produce results that are too optimistic. Common problems:

- **Look-ahead bias**: using information that was not available at the time. For example, financial statements are published several months after the fiscal year ends, index members are known only afterwards, and data are later revised.
- Survivorship bias (survivorship bias): using only stocks or funds that still exist, missing those that were delisted or closed.
- **Overfitting**: trying many rules and parameters on the same data and picking the best. The chosen rule fits the noise in these data (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/#anomalies, Lesson 4.10, "Estimation Error and Robust Optimization" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-10-estimation-error/#error-maximization).
- Trading costs, taxes and market impact: backtests often ignore them, and high-turnover strategies suffer most.
- Changing conditions: interest rates, market structure and participants change, and patterns that worked in the past may stop working.

> **Check question C4**
> 
> A backtest picks stocks every December 31 by the companies' earnings growth for that full year and buys them the same day. The main problem with this backtest is:
> 
> (A) Look-ahead bias: full-year earnings are known only when the annual report comes out the next year
> (B) Survivorship bias
> (C) Turnover is too low
> (D) There is no problem; earnings growth is public information
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

Ways to reduce these problems: use only data available at the time (by publication date, not by accounting period), use databases that include delisted securities, deduct realistic costs; fix the rules in advance, choose parameters on one stretch of data and test on another stretch not used before (out-of-sample testing, out of sample), or proceed on a rolling basis through time; and record how many rules were tried in all.

> **Check question C5**
> 
> If a strategy's parameters are tuned to be optimal on all the historical data and its Sharpe ratio is then computed on the same data, that Sharpe ratio is an unbiased estimate of its future Sharpe ratio.
> 
> (True or false)
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

## Summary

- Monte Carlo simulation generates many paths from an assumed distribution to give the distribution of wealth, its percentiles and the probability of reaching a goal.
- The mean of wealth $e^{\mu t}$ is above the median $e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}$, and the gap grows with volatility; planning should look at the median and low percentiles.
- Results depend on the assumed distribution, parameters and correlations; the bootstrap keeps fat tails, and adding parameter uncertainty widens long-run ranges.
- Common biases in backtests: look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, overfitting, ignoring costs, changing conditions; test out of sample.

## Exercises

Assign them after the lesson. Answers and grading points are in the key file.

**Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)**

An adviser plans for a 35-year-old client: "You invest 100,000 dollars now; stocks average 7% a year, so in 30 years you'll have $100{,}000 \times 1.07^{30} \approx 761{,}000$ dollars; with your other savings, the 400,000-dollar part of your retirement goal is certainly covered." Assume yearly log returns are independent and normal, with a mean annual return μ = 7% and a volatility of 18% (compute the mean with continuous compounding, $e^{\mu t}$).
(a) What are the median and the mean of wealth after 30 years (in thousands of dollars)?
(b) What is the probability that wealth is below 400,000 dollars? Evaluate the adviser's statement.

**Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)**

Simulate 30 years with the assumptions of Figure 1-1 (μ = 7%, σ = 18%). In fact μ is an estimate with a standard error of 2 points. If each path first draws a μ from a normal distribution with mean 7% and standard deviation 2% and then simulates returns, the variance of 30-year log wealth is about $\sigma^2 T + (\text{SE} \times T)^2$.
(a) Without and with parameter uncertainty, what is the standard deviation of 30-year log wealth? In each case, what is the 5% percentile of wealth per dollar invested (with the median at $e^{1.614}$)?
(b) Why does parameter uncertainty matter so much for long-run outcomes? What does this imply for 30-year retirement planning, and for the claim in Lesson 4.12, "Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-12-lifecycle-allocation/ that long-term investors should hold more stocks?

**Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)**

A firm markets a momentum strategy: "We backtested 20 years using the current S&P 500 members: each month we buy the 50 stocks that rose most over the past 12 months. The annualized return was 18%, against 10% for the index, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.2." The material mentions that the parameters (12 months, 50 stocks, monthly rebalancing) were chosen from 200 combinations; the backtest deducts no trading costs; and monthly turnover is about 60%.
(a) If each unit of turnover (selling and buying) costs about 0.3%, about how many percentage points a year do trading costs come to?
(b) Identify the biases in this backtest, and for each say whether it pushes the result up or down, and why. Evaluate the firm's claim.

**Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)**

A strategy has an in-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.2 over 10 years and an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.3 over the next 5 years. The standard error of an estimated annual Sharpe ratio is about $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ ($T$ in years).
(a) What are the standard errors of the in-sample and out-of-sample Sharpe ratios? What is the t-value of their difference (the two periods are independent)?
(b) One colleague says: "Out of sample it's only 0.3, so the strategy has stopped working." Another says: "5 years is too short; the out-of-sample result says nothing, so trust the in-sample 1.2." Evaluate each. Then, on plausibility: what does a Sharpe ratio of 1.2 for a simple strategy suggest, compared with the market's Sharpe ratio (about 0.3 to 0.4)?
